lessons.title: Write your first effective image prompts in ChatGPT and Gemini
lessons.summary: Learn the anatomy of a strong image prompt for GPT Image 2 in ChatGPT and native image generation in the Gemini app so your generations look intentional on the first or second try instead of random.
lessons.goal: Write a structured image prompt in ChatGPT or the Gemini app that reliably produces a usable, on-brief image without a dozen wasted generations.
lessons.whyItMatters: Both ChatGPT's GPT Image 2 and Gemini's native image generation sit right in the chat window, so it's tempting to type something quick like "a nice photo of a coffee shop" and hope. Vague prompts like that produce random, generic results that force you to regenerate over and over, guessing at what might work — and every regeneration counts against your plan's usage. GPT Image 2 is a reasoning-based model that plans composition and text layout before it renders, which means it rewards a prompt built from the same repeatable structure — subject, setting, composition, lighting, style, mood, format — far more than a vague one-liner, and Gemini's image model responds to the same structure. Learning this once means faster, more predictable results in whichever tool you open.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have a ChatGPT account open (chatgpt.com, the desktop app, or mobile) or the Gemini app open (gemini.google.com or mobile) — image generation is built directly into the chat composer in both; you don't need a separate tool, plugin, or paid plan to try this.
steps: Before writing anything, decide the single subject and the single action or state of that subject — one clear idea, not three ideas combined.
Build the prompt in this order: subject, setting/background, composition (shot type and angle), lighting, art or photographic style, mood/color palette, then technical notes (aspect ratio, format).

Replace vague adjectives ("beautiful," "amazing," "professional") with concrete, specific nouns and camera or art-direction language ("golden-hour side lighting," "medium shot at eye level," "flat illustration with muted pastels").
State the aspect ratio and destination format explicitly (square for Instagram feed, 16:9 for a website hero, vertical for Stories) — both ChatGPT and Gemini follow an explicit ratio instruction.
Type the prompt directly into the ChatGPT or Gemini chat composer and generate the image.
Compare the result line by line against your prompt to see which phrase produced which visual result.
Reply in the same conversation asking to change only the one weakest line — both tools support this kind of in-chat follow-up edit — rather than starting a new chat with a rewritten prompt.
Save the working prompt as a reusable template for the next similar image.
lessons.prompt:
[SUBJECT — who or what, with specific identifying details], [KEY ACTION OR POSE], [SETTING/BACKGROUND], [COMPOSITION — shot type and camera angle], [LIGHTING], [ART STYLE OR PHOTOGRAPHIC STYLE], [MOOD/COLOR PALETTE], [ASPECT RATIO / FORMAT NOTES]

Example filled in:
A barista in her 30s steaming milk behind an espresso machine, mid-action with steam visibly rising, inside a small independent coffee shop with exposed brick and hanging plants, medium shot at eye level, warm morning sunlight streaming through a front window, photorealistic editorial photography, cozy and inviting mood with warm amber tones, square 1:1 format for Instagram
lessons.explanation: The fixed order (subject, setting, composition, lighting, style, mood, format) works because GPT Image 2 is built to reason through composition and layout before it renders — leaving out a category doesn't just skip it, it leaves the model to guess, which is where generic results come from. Gemini's image model rewards the same structure. Concrete nouns and camera language beat vague adjectives because "beautiful" has no visual definition for either model to render, while "medium shot, eye level, golden-hour side lighting" describes an actual, renderable scene. Naming the destination format up front saves a wasted regeneration cycle just to fix the crop.
lessons.example:
Input: a request for a hero image for a bakery's website with no other direction.

Weak prompt, typed into ChatGPT or Gemini: "a nice photo of a bakery" — produces a generic, unusable stock-photo-style image that could be any bakery anywhere.

Strong prompt (using the template): "A wooden pastry display case filled with croissants and sourdough loaves, close-up composition at a slight downward angle, soft diffused window light from the left, photorealistic food photography, warm and rustic mood with golden-brown tones, 16:9 for a website hero banner." Typed into either tool, this produces a specific, composed shot that looks like it was art-directed rather than guessed at.
lessons.exercise: In ChatGPT or the Gemini app, write one prompt using the template above for a real image you currently need (a work project, a social post, or a personal use case), generate it, then reply in the same conversation asking it to fix just the weakest line and regenerate.
lessons.expectedResult: Two generations from the same base prompt in the same conversation: the first a reasonable first draft, the second visibly improved in exactly the one area you targeted — proof that you can now steer the output instead of rerolling blindly.
commonMistakes: Using vague adjectives like "stunning" or "professional" instead of specific, renderable details.
Combining more than one subject or action in a single prompt, which forces the model to split its attention and blur the composition.
Forgetting to specify aspect ratio, then having to crop or regenerate to fit the destination platform.
Starting a brand-new chat and rewriting the entire prompt to fix one small issue, instead of asking for a targeted change in the same conversation and losing the context of what was already working.
lessons.proTip: Keep a running "swipe file" of prompt fragments that reliably produced a look you liked (a lighting phrase, a style descriptor) so you can drop them into new prompts in either tool instead of reinventing your vocabulary each time.

lessons.title: Choose between ChatGPT and Gemini for image generation
lessons.summary: Match a specific image task to GPT Image 2 in ChatGPT or native image generation in Gemini — the two tools you'll reach for most of the time — instead of defaulting to whatever you already have open.
lessons.goal: Pick ChatGPT or Gemini as your primary tool for a given image task, with the other as backup, based on what each is actually best at.
lessons.whyItMatters: ChatGPT and Gemini both do serious image generation now, but they aren't identical tools wearing different skins. GPT Image 2, OpenAI's current image model in ChatGPT, is the first reasoning-based image model — it plans composition and text layout before rendering, and as of mid-2026 it leads blind-vote arenas for prompt adherence and photorealism, with excellent text rendering and iterative in-chat editing. Gemini's native image model is best-in-class for infographics, diagrams, and mockups, edits conversationally, and sits inside a Google Workspace-connected app, so it's a natural fit when your work already lives in Docs, Slides, or Sheets. Picking the wrong one for the job means fighting the tool instead of using it.
steps: Write down the actual job before opening either tool: what is the image for, does it need legible text baked in, does it need to feel like a diagram or infographic, and is it already part of a Google Workspace or ChatGPT workflow?
If the brief is complex and needs precise instruction-following, photorealism, or a lot of text placed accurately, lead with ChatGPT (GPT Image 2).
If the image is an infographic, diagram, mockup, or anything that benefits from clean information layout, lead with Gemini.
If you're already deep in a Google Doc, Slide deck, or Sheet, or want to hand the image off to Veo afterward for a short animated clip, lead with Gemini.
If you're already in a ChatGPT Project with reference files or custom instructions for the brand, lead with ChatGPT to keep everything in one thread.
For anything genuinely uncertain, generate a first draft in your primary pick, then run the same brief in the other tool as a fast second opinion before you commit real time to refining one version.
Use the prompt below to get a grounded recommendation before you commit for a high-stakes job.
lessons.prompt:
I need to generate an image for the following job. Based only on the tool strengths I list below (do not add or invent other tools or capabilities), tell me which ONE tool is the best primary choice — ChatGPT or Gemini — with a one-sentence reason, plus one sentence on when I'd reach for the other instead.

Job: [DESCRIBE THE IMAGE TASK — e.g., "a polished hero banner for an ecommerce site that needs a legible headline baked into the image"]

Tool strengths:
- ChatGPT (GPT Image 2): reasoning-based image model that plans composition and text layout before rendering; leads on prompt adherence and photorealism, with excellent text rendering; supports iterative in-chat editing — describe a change and regenerate in the same conversation; can pull in reference files and custom instructions from a ChatGPT Project.
- Gemini (native image generation in the Gemini app): best-in-class for infographics, diagrams, and mockups; edits conversationally in plain language; integrated with Google Workspace (Docs, Slides, Sheets) so it can work directly against documents you already have open; a generated image can be handed to Veo as a first frame for a short animated clip.

Recommend based only on the strengths listed above.
lessons.explanation: Giving the assistant the tool-strength facts directly (rather than asking it to recall them from memory) keeps the recommendation grounded in what's actually true instead of an outdated or invented comparison — image tools change fast enough that even a well-informed assistant's memory can lag. Asking for both a primary and a "when to switch" note matters in practice: your first-choice tool might be the wrong fit for one variant of the job even within the same brief. The one-sentence reason requirement forces a real justification you can sanity-check rather than an unexplained pick.
lessons.example:
Job: "a polished hero banner for an ecommerce site that needs a legible headline baked into the image."

Expected recommendation: primary — ChatGPT (GPT Image 2), because it leads on instruction-following and text rendering, which is exactly what a headline baked directly into the image needs; switch to Gemini instead if the banner needs to double as a labeled infographic-style graphic rather than a photographic hero shot.
lessons.exercise: In ChatGPT or Gemini (whichever you use less), run this prompt with a real image task you have coming up, then generate the first draft in the recommended tool.
lessons.expectedResult: A specific ChatGPT-or-Gemini recommendation tied to the actual requirements of your job, and a first image generated in the recommended tool rather than your default habit.
commonMistakes: Always defaulting to whichever app you already have open, even when the job specifically needs the other tool's strength.
Ignoring that a job already living in Google Docs or Slides is a natural fit for Gemini instead of exporting and re-importing between apps.
Assuming both tools handle dense, labeled infographic text equally well.
Not running the same brief in both quickly when the choice is genuinely unclear, and overthinking a call that a two-minute test would resolve.
lessons.proTip: Build a one-page internal reference table mapping your team's common job types to ChatGPT or Gemini as the default, so this decision doesn't have to be re-litigated for every new request.

lessons.title: Iterate on an image: refine and vary through conversational edits
lessons.summary: Take a first-draft image through targeted refinement and variation using ChatGPT's and Gemini's in-chat editing, instead of regenerating from scratch every time something is almost right.
lessons.goal: Turn a promising first-draft image into a final, usable asset using targeted in-chat edits instead of full re-generations.
lessons.whyItMatters: The first generation is almost never the final image — but rewriting the whole prompt every time one detail is wrong wastes your usage allowance and throws away the parts that were already working. Both ChatGPT and Gemini let you keep editing the same image turn by turn in one conversation: GPT Image 2 supports iterative in-chat editing, and Gemini's image model edits conversationally from plain-language instructions. Learning to isolate a single change and generate a couple of close variations of a keeper — instead of starting a new chat with a rewritten prompt every time — is the difference between a fast, professional iteration loop and an expensive trial-and-error habit.
steps: Generate a baseline image from your structured prompt and evaluate it honestly: what's right, what's wrong, and is the core composition worth keeping.
If the composition is right but one element is wrong, reply in the same chat with a targeted refinement instruction rather than rewriting the full prompt or starting a new conversation.

State explicitly what to preserve (composition, subject, color palette, style) alongside what to change — both tools will otherwise treat an edit as license to regenerate more of the scene than you wanted.
Once one version is close, ask for 2-3 variations of that specific image in the same thread, rather than opening a new chat and generating fresh random attempts.
Pick the strongest variation and ask for it at the highest resolution or quality setting the tool offers before you export.
Check the final version at full size for artifacts (warped hands, garbled small text, odd seams) before exporting.
Download or save at the resolution and format your destination actually requires.
lessons.prompt:
Keep everything about this image the same except: [SPECIFIC ELEMENT TO CHANGE].

Do not change: [ELEMENTS TO PRESERVE — e.g., "composition, subject pose, color palette, overall style"].

Change instruction: [SPECIFIC CHANGE — e.g., "replace the background with a plain white studio backdrop" / "make the lighting brighter and remove the shadow on the left side of the subject"].
lessons.explanation: Naming what to preserve is what stops a small fix from becoming a full re-roll — without it, both ChatGPT and Gemini will sometimes treat an instruction as license to regenerate more of the scene than you asked for, and you lose the composition you already liked. Isolating one change per pass, sent as a follow-up in the same conversation, also makes it possible to tell exactly which instruction caused which visual result — which is what makes iteration a controllable process instead of a guessing game. Asking for the highest resolution or quality only once, on the version you've already confirmed is right, avoids spending that step on a draft you'll end up discarding.
lessons.example:
Baseline image: a product flat-lay with the right composition and lighting, but a distracting patterned background, generated in ChatGPT.

Refinement prompt, sent as a follow-up in the same chat: "Keep everything about this image the same except: the background. Do not change: the product, its position, the lighting, or the color palette. Change instruction: replace the patterned background with a plain matte white surface."

Expected result: the same product shot, same framing and light, with only the background swapped — not a fresh, differently composed image.
lessons.exercise: In ChatGPT or Gemini, take an image you generated in a previous lesson (or a fresh draft) and run it through one targeted refinement in the same conversation, then ask for 2-3 variations of the improved version, then request the highest-quality export.
lessons.expectedResult: A final image that kept the composition and details you liked from the original draft, with only the specific flaw corrected, at full export resolution with no visible artifacts.
commonMistakes: Starting a brand-new chat and rewriting the entire prompt to fix a small issue, which loses the image as context and discards everything that was already working.
Not keeping the refinement conversation intact, making it hard to return to a keeper image later for another variation.
Requesting the highest-resolution export before the composition is finalized, wasting the step on a version you'll end up discarding.
Skipping the full-size artifact check and exporting an image with a flaw only visible at full resolution.
lessons.proTip: Keep the whole iteration for one image in a single ChatGPT or Gemini conversation, and rename or save that chat once you land on a keeper — so returning to it for a future variation is one click away instead of trying to reconstruct the prompt from memory.

lessons.title: Generate product photos and mockups with ChatGPT and Gemini
lessons.summary: Produce believable product photography and mockups from a real product photo or accurate description, without misrepresenting what you actually sell.
lessons.goal: Generate an accurate, platform-ready product photo or mockup for a real product without adding features, colors, or details it doesn't have.
lessons.whyItMatters: Small businesses and independent sellers can't afford a studio shoot for every SKU, color variant, or seasonal mockup. Generating product photography directly in ChatGPT or Gemini closes that gap fast — but a generated image that quietly adds a feature, changes a color, or invents a logo becomes a return, a complaint, or a marketplace policy violation instead of a time-saver. The discipline here is generating photography that looks professional while staying strictly accurate to the real product.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have a real photo of the product ready to upload — both ChatGPT and Gemini accept image uploads directly in the chat (ChatGPT takes JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP files; Gemini accepts images as part of its multimodal input) — plus the exact, accurate product details: material, color, dimensions, and any text or logo that actually appears on it.
steps: List the product's exact, verified attributes — material, color, size, distinguishing features — before writing the prompt.
Choose a real-world context that matches how the product will actually be sold: plain studio background, lifestyle scene, flat lay, or on-model.
Match your destination platform's photography conventions (many marketplaces require a pure white background for the primary listing image; social and lifestyle content allows more styling).
Upload the actual product photo as an attachment in the ChatGPT or Gemini chat so the generated version stays visually consistent with what a buyer receives.
Generate multiple angles or contexts from the same accurate description in the same conversation.
Compare every generated image against the real product and reject any version that alters proportions, adds unlisted features, or invents branding.
Export at the resolution your marketplace or website requires.
lessons.prompt:
Using the attached reference photo of [PRODUCT NAME] (if provided), create a product photo of a [MATERIAL/COLOR/KEY FEATURES — be exact, include only what is true of the real product].

Context: [e.g., "held in a hand against a neutral studio background" / "on a rustic wooden table with morning light" / "flat lay on a marble surface with 2-3 complementary props"].

Style: clean e-commerce product photography, [BACKGROUND COLOR/TYPE], soft even lighting, sharp focus on the product, realistic minimal shadow.

Rules: Do not add any feature, color, logo, or accessory the product does not actually have. Do not alter the product's proportions or shape. Format: [ASPECT RATIO for your platform, e.g., 1:1 for a marketplace listing].
lessons.explanation: Listing exact, verified attributes before writing the creative direction is what stops the model from filling gaps with plausible-but-wrong details — the same guardrail principle used for any AI-assisted factual work, applied to a physical product. Uploading the real photo grounds GPT Image 2's composition planning, or Gemini's generation, in what the product actually looks like instead of a guess from text alone. Matching platform conventions (pure white background for a primary marketplace image, styled lifestyle for social) means the output is usable without a redo. The explicit "do not add" rule doesn't guarantee accuracy on its own, which is why the manual comparison-against-the-real-product step stays in the workflow rather than being skipped.
lessons.example:
Product: "a hand-poured soy candle in a clear amber glass jar, 8oz, natural cotton wick, no label text."

Context: flat lay on a light wood surface with a small sprig of dried lavender and a folded linen cloth, soft natural light from the side.

Expected output, generated in ChatGPT or Gemini with the real candle photo attached: a clean flat-lay photo of an amber glass jar candle matching the exact size and material described, with no invented label, no wrong jar shape, and no colors not present on the real product — ready to compare directly against the physical candle before use.
lessons.exercise: In ChatGPT or Gemini, generate a product photo or mockup for one real product you sell or are launching, using its exact attributes and an uploaded reference photo, then compare the result against the actual item.
lessons.expectedResult: A platform-ready product image that matches the real product's material, color, and proportions exactly, with no invented branding or features.
commonMistakes: Skipping the image upload when you have a real product photo available, leading to a "similar but wrong" product.
Not matching the background requirements of the destination marketplace, causing a listing rejection.
Generating a logo or label that doesn't match your real branding and using it without noticing.
Publishing AI-generated product images without checking your marketplace's policy on AI-generated listing photos, or without disclosure where required.
lessons.proTip: Build one reusable lighting-and-background prompt block, save it as a ChatGPT Project instruction or in a Gemini Gem, and reuse it across your entire catalog so every product photo looks like it came from the same shoot.

lessons.title: Create social and marketing visuals with a consistent brand style in ChatGPT and Gemini
lessons.summary: Produce a set of on-brand social or marketing visuals that look like one campaign instead of a series of unrelated one-off generations.
lessons.goal: Generate a batch of social or marketing images that share one consistent, recognizable visual style.
lessons.whyItMatters: Inconsistent visuals are one of the fastest ways to weaken brand recognition — a feed where every post looks like it came from a different designer trains an audience to scroll past instead of recognize you. Marketers and social media managers who post regularly need a repeatable way to keep dozens of images visually aligned without manually re-describing the same style every time, which is where small wording drift quietly creeps in. ChatGPT Projects (which store custom instructions and files for every chat inside them) and Gemini Gems (saved, reusable custom personas and instructions) are built exactly for this: bake the style block in once and stop retyping it.
steps: Define a reusable "style block": a fixed description of color palette, art style, lighting, and mood that represents your brand.
Write one master prompt template that separates the fixed style block from a variable subject line for each specific post.
Reuse the exact style block wording for every image in the set — don't paraphrase it between generations, even slightly.
Save the style block as a ChatGPT Project's custom instructions, or as a saved Gemini Gem, so it's included automatically instead of retyped.
Set one consistent aspect ratio per platform and stick to it across the batch (e.g., all feed posts at 4:5, all Stories at 9:16).
If your tool supports a reference image or attached example, upload one approved image to lock the look further.
Batch-generate the week's or campaign's variants using the same style block and format, in the same Project or Gem.
Review the full set side by side, not one image at a time, to catch any visual drift before publishing.
lessons.prompt:
Use this exact style block for every image in this set — do not vary it:
Style block: [e.g., "flat illustration, muted pastel palette (dusty blue, terracotta, cream), soft rounded shapes, minimal shadows, warm and approachable mood"]

Now generate an image of: [SPECIFIC SUBJECT FOR THIS POST — e.g., "a person unboxing a package at their kitchen table"]

Format: [ASPECT RATIO for platform, e.g., 4:5 for Instagram feed / 9:16 for Stories]

Do not introduce any new colors, styles, or moods outside the style block above.
lessons.explanation: Separating an immutable style block from a variable subject line is what keeps a whole week or month of content visually consistent — the subject changes every time, the style never does. Reusing the identical style block wording matters more than it seems: even small paraphrasing changes how either model interprets tone and palette, which is how a "consistent" set of posts quietly drifts by post six. Saving the style block as a ChatGPT Project instruction or a Gemini Gem removes the retyping step entirely, so drift caused by a mistyped or half-remembered style block stops being possible. Reviewing the set side by side rather than one at a time is the only reliable way to catch remaining drift before it reaches your audience.
lessons.example:
Style block: "bold flat illustration, high-contrast orange and navy palette, thick outlines, playful geometric shapes, energetic mood."

Week's subjects: "a customer opening a laptop at a coffee shop," "a team celebrating around a whiteboard," "a hand pressing a button on a phone screen."

Expected output, generated from the same ChatGPT Project or Gemini Gem: three distinct images that share the exact same palette, line weight, and mood — recognizably one campaign — rather than three visually unrelated illustrations that happen to share a subject theme.
lessons.exercise: In ChatGPT or Gemini, write one style block for a brand or campaign you work on, save it as a Project instruction or a Gem, then generate three different post subjects using it, and lay all three side by side to check consistency.
lessons.expectedResult: Three (or more) images that are clearly part of the same visual system — same palette, style, and mood — differing only in subject matter.
commonMistakes: Rewriting the style description slightly for each new prompt instead of saving it once, which causes gradual visual drift across the set.
Mixing multiple aspect ratios within one campaign, making the feed or story sequence look disjointed.
Reviewing each image individually instead of as a set, missing drift that's only obvious side by side.
Forgetting platform-specific safe zones for text overlays when generating images meant to have captions added later.
lessons.proTip: Save your style block as a ChatGPT Project's custom instructions or as a Gemini Gem, so every new chat in that Project or Gem starts with the style baked in — removing any chance of retyping it slightly differently.

lessons.title: Use ChatGPT and Gemini for text in images and graphic design work
lessons.summary: Generate images with accurate, legible text for posters, quote graphics, and simple design work in ChatGPT or Gemini, and know when to finish the text by hand instead.
lessons.goal: Generate a graphic with correctly spelled, well-placed text, and know when to hand off text rendering to a design tool instead.
lessons.whyItMatters: Text inside AI-generated images has historically been the weakest point of these tools, and while GPT Image 2 and Gemini's image model have both gotten far more reliable at it — GPT Image 2 as a reasoning model that plans text layout before rendering, and Gemini as a strong performer for text-in-image work like infographics and labeled mockups — a single misspelled word or garbled letterform in a client-facing poster or ad still ships as a visible error if you don't proofread it. Knowing which tool to reach for, how to prompt for text, and when to fall back to manual typography keeps design work fast without risking an embarrassing mistake.
steps: Keep any requested text short — a few words per line, not full sentences — since accuracy drops as text length grows.
Specify text placement and hierarchy explicitly (headline large at the top, subtext smaller below) rather than leaving layout to the model.
Write out the exact text in quotation marks so there's no ambiguity about wording or spelling.
For a headline-driven poster or quote graphic, lead with ChatGPT (GPT Image 2); for a labeled diagram or infographic, lead with Gemini.
Generate the graphic, then proofread every character against your exact intended wording — don't skim it.
If the text still isn't rendering reliably after a couple of attempts, generate the background and imagery without text, and add the text afterward in a design tool for guaranteed accuracy.
lessons.prompt:
Design a [POSTER / QUOTE GRAPHIC / SOCIAL GRAPHIC] with the following text rendered exactly as written, no spelling changes:
Headline (large, top third): "[EXACT TEXT]"
Subtext (smaller, below headline): "[EXACT TEXT]"

Visual style: [DESCRIBE — color palette, imagery, typography feel, e.g., "bold sans-serif lettering, high-contrast navy and gold, minimalist geometric background"]

Layout: [e.g., "centered text over a plain background, generous margins"]

Do not add any additional text, watermark, or logo beyond what is specified above.
lessons.explanation: Quoting the exact text and separating it into an explicit headline/subtext hierarchy is what both models key off — an unstructured request like "add some motivational text" gives far more room to misspell or mis-lay-out the words. Keeping the text short is a direct accuracy lever: every additional word compounds the chance of an error somewhere in the line. The instruction to add no extra text or watermark closes off either model's tendency to fill empty space with invented lettering.
lessons.example:
Request: headline "NEW SEASON, NEW YOU" and subtext "20% off all classes this week" on a minimalist fitness studio promo graphic, bold sans-serif, high-contrast teal and white.

Expected output, generated in ChatGPT: a graphic with both lines legible and spelled exactly as given, headline dominant at the top, subtext smaller below it — which you then proofread letter by letter before publishing, since even a strong text-rendering model can occasionally drop or duplicate a character.
lessons.exercise: In ChatGPT or Gemini, generate one text-bearing graphic using this prompt with a real headline you need, and proofread the output character by character against your intended wording.
lessons.expectedResult: A graphic with legible, correctly spelled text in the right hierarchy and placement — or, if the text failed, a clear signal to fall back to a design tool for that element.
commonMistakes: Requesting a full paragraph of body text, which remains unreliable across both tools.
Skipping the letter-by-letter proofread and publishing on the assumption the text is correct.

Using the tool least suited to the layout — a headline-heavy poster generally does better in ChatGPT, a labeled diagram generally does better in Gemini — without checking which is actually working for your specific graphic.
Treating an AI-generated logo as safe to trademark or use commercially without a human design and legal review.
lessons.proTip: For anything client-facing, generate the background and imagery with ChatGPT or Gemini and drop in real vector text using a design tool afterward — it costs one extra step and removes all spelling risk.

lessons.title: Commercial safety: using ChatGPT and Gemini images for paid and client work
lessons.summary: Evaluate whether a ChatGPT or Gemini generated image is safe to use commercially and choose a plan tier and workflow that matches your organization's actual risk tolerance.
lessons.goal: Run a specific commercial-use case through a risk checklist and determine what licensing or documentation step it needs before it ships.
lessons.whyItMatters: Not every commercial image job carries the same risk, and ChatGPT and Gemini don't automatically remove that risk just because they're the two mainstream tools you already have open. ChatGPT's Business and Enterprise plans exclude your data from model training, and Google's Workspace Business and Enterprise editions add admin controls and data governance that the free consumer tiers don't have — so plan tier matters as much as tool choice. For comparison, Adobe Firefly's enterprise plan is the one mainstream AI image tool that offers formal IP indemnification and attaches provenance metadata to its outputs; neither ChatGPT nor Gemini currently offers an equivalent guarantee on their standard consumer, Plus, or Pro plans, which is exactly why a manual risk checklist matters more, not less, when a ChatGPT or Gemini image is heading into paid or client work.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Know which ChatGPT and/or Gemini plan your organization is actually on — Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, or Enterprise for ChatGPT; Free, Google AI Pro, Google AI Ultra, or a Workspace Business/Enterprise edition for Gemini — since commercial usage rights and data-handling guarantees differ by tier even within the same product.
steps: Classify the use case by risk level: internal draft or mockup, versus public paid campaign, versus a trademarked logo or packaging asset.

Check whether your specific ChatGPT or Gemini plan tier (not just the tool in general) says anything about commercial usage and training-data exclusion — ChatGPT Business and Enterprise, for instance, exclude your data from model training; lower tiers may not.
Don't assume either tool offers formal IP indemnification the way some enterprise-focused image tools do — budget for your own legal review on anything high-stakes.
Avoid generating recognizable real people, real brand logos, or copyrighted characters without explicit rights, regardless of which tool you're using.
Avoid naming a specific living artist's style in a prompt for client or paid work.
Log the tool (ChatGPT or Gemini), plan tier, and generation date for any asset used in a paid campaign, so you have a record if a claim ever arises.
For genuinely high-stakes, brand-critical, or heavily regulated commercial work, treat the AI-generated image as a strong draft that a human designer and your legal team sign off on before it ships.
lessons.prompt:
I'm about to use an AI-generated image for the following purpose. Based only on the facts I provide below, flag any commercial-safety risks and tell me what to check before I publish.

Intended use: [e.g., "paid Instagram ad campaign" / "internal slide deck" / "printed retail packaging"]
Tool used: [ChatGPT or Gemini]
My plan/tier: [e.g., "ChatGPT Plus" / "ChatGPT Business" / "Gemini Free" / "Google AI Pro" / "Workspace Enterprise"]
Does the image include: a recognizable real person? [yes/no] a real brand's logo or product? [yes/no] a likely-copyrighted character, or a style reference naming a specific living artist or studio? [yes/no]

List the specific risks given only these facts, and tell me what documentation or licensing check I should do before this ships.
lessons.explanation: Feeding the assistant only the facts you supply — rather than letting it improvise legal claims about a tool's licensing terms — keeps the risk assessment grounded in what you actually know instead of a plausible-sounding guess about copyright law. Separating plan tier from tool name matters because commercial and data-handling terms frequently differ between a personal ChatGPT Plus or Gemini Free account and a Business or Enterprise subscription to the same product. The explicit yes/no checks for real people, real logos, and named-artist style references target the three most common sources of an actual claim.
lessons.example:
Intended use: paid Instagram ad campaign. Tool: ChatGPT, plan: ChatGPT Plus. No real person or logo, but the prompt referenced "in the style of [a specific living illustrator]."

Expected flagged risks: the named-artist style reference as a potential rights issue independent of the tool itself, plus a note that a personal ChatGPT Plus plan doesn't carry the data-exclusion or governance guarantees of a Business or Enterprise plan — and a recommendation to remove the named-artist reference and, for an ongoing paid campaign, consider moving the account to a Business or Enterprise tier.
lessons.exercise: In ChatGPT or Gemini, run this checklist prompt against one real image (or planned image) you intend to use commercially, and act on whatever it flags.
lessons.expectedResult: A specific, fact-grounded list of commercial-safety risks for your actual use case, plus a clear next step (a licensing check, a plan-tier upgrade, or a documentation note) before the asset ships.
commonMistakes: Assuming a personal ChatGPT Plus or Gemini Google AI Pro subscription automatically grants the same commercial protections as a Business or Enterprise plan.
Naming a specific living artist's style in a prompt for client or paid work.
Using AI-generated images of recognizable real people without their consent or a release.
Skipping documentation of which tool (ChatGPT or Gemini) and plan tier generated a paid-campaign asset, leaving no record if a claim arises later.
lessons.proTip: For any high-stakes paid campaign or trademark-adjacent asset, treat ChatGPT and Gemini output as a strong first draft, not a legally cleared final asset — and budget time for a human design and legal pass before anything ships to a client or the public.

lessons.title: Build a repeatable AI image creative pipeline with ChatGPT and Gemini
lessons.summary: Turn everything from prompt structure to tool selection to commercial-safety checks into one documented, reusable process for every new image request.
lessons.goal: Document a standard, repeatable pipeline that takes any new image request from brief to finished, on-brand, correctly checked asset without starting from scratch each time.
lessons.whyItMatters: Anyone generating images regularly — weekly social content, monthly product drops, recurring campaign assets — eventually needs a system, not a fresh round of one-off prompting every time. A documented pipeline ties together prompt structure, ChatGPT-vs-Gemini tool selection, brand consistency (via Projects and Gems), iteration workflow, text handling, and commercial-safety checks into a single reference so the process survives a new hire, a plan-tier change, or simply your own memory on a busy week.
steps: Document your standard brief template: the fields you fill in for every image request (use case, platform, dimensions, deadline).

Document your default tool per job type: e.g., product photos in ChatGPT with an uploaded reference photo; infographics and diagrams in Gemini; headline-driven posters in ChatGPT; anything already living in a Google Doc or Slide in Gemini.
Maintain a saved style block library — as ChatGPT Project custom instructions and/or Gemini Gems, one per brand or campaign — so visual consistency doesn't depend on remembering exact wording.
Define your standard iteration workflow: draft, targeted refinement in the same conversation, 2-3 variations of the keeper, highest-quality export only at the end.
Define your text/typography handoff rule: which tool you use for text-heavy work, and when you fall back to manual typography instead.
Define your commercial-safety checklist, including plan tier per tool, as a gate every asset passes through before it ships, not an afterthought.
Set a file naming and logging convention (tool, plan tier, prompt, date) so any asset is traceable later.
After one full cycle using the pipeline, review it and tighten whichever step caused the most friction.
lessons.prompt:
Help me draft a one-page creative image pipeline document for my [ROLE/BUSINESS]. Use this structure and fill it in using only the details I give you — do not invent tools, budgets, or team members I haven't mentioned:

1. Standard brief template (fields we fill in for every image request)
2. Default tool per job type: [LIST YOUR JOB TYPES AND PREFERRED TOOLS, e.g., "product photos: ChatGPT; infographics and diagrams: Gemini; headline-driven posters: ChatGPT"]
3. Brand style block(s) and where they're saved: [PASTE YOUR STYLE BLOCK(S) AND NOTE WHETHER IT'S A CHATGPT PROJECT OR A GEMINI GEM]
4. Iteration workflow: [DESCRIBE YOUR STEPS, e.g., "draft, refine in the same chat, generate 3 variations, export at highest quality"]
5. Text/typography rule: [YOUR RULE]
6. Commercial-safety checklist, including plan tier per tool: [YOUR CHECKLIST ITEMS]
7. File naming and log format: [YOUR CONVENTION]

Write it as a clean one-page reference doc, organized under these 7 headings.
lessons.explanation: Restricting the assistant to only the details you supply keeps the resulting document an accurate reflection of your real process rather than a generic template padded with invented tools or steps you don't actually use. Structuring it under the same seven areas covered across this path (prompting, ChatGPT-vs-Gemini selection, brand consistency, iteration, text, safety, traceability) means the document isn't a new idea — it's the existing skills from this path made durable and shareable rather than something you have to re-derive from memory on every new request.
lessons.example:
Input: job types are "product photos," "weekly social graphics," and "quarterly campaign posters," with a saved ChatGPT Project for the brand's Instagram look and a rule that all client-facing text is added manually in a design tool.

Expected output: a one-page document with those exact job types mapped to ChatGPT or Gemini, the ChatGPT Project noted under section 3, the manual-text rule stated plainly under section 5, and no invented team members, budgets, or tools beyond what was provided.
lessons.exercise: In ChatGPT or Gemini, fill in this prompt using your real answers from the tool-selection, style-block, iteration, and safety-checklist lessons in this path, generate the document, and save it somewhere your team can reference it.
lessons.expectedResult: A one-page pipeline reference document you can hand to yourself or a teammate that shortens the time from "new image request" to "finished, safe, on-brand asset."
commonMistakes: Skipping documentation because the process feels obvious right now — it stops being obvious after a few months or a team change.
Letting the pipeline go stale as either tool updates its models or features, instead of revisiting the default-tool section periodically.
Not logging plan tier per tool, which breaks the commercial-safety net the pipeline is supposed to provide.
Building the pipeline as a private habit instead of a shared document the rest of the team can actually use.
lessons.proTip: Revisit the pipeline document quarterly — ChatGPT and Gemini both ship new image-generation features often enough that this quarter's default tool per job type may no longer be the right call next quarter.
